paragraphs: Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, whom we left knocking at the strong, locked gates of the widow Morozov’s house, naturally ended by making himself heard. Fenya was still shaken by the fright she had had two hours earlier, and too “upset” to go to bed. The furious knocking at the gate nearly sent her into hysterics. She had seen him drive away herself, but she imagined it must be Dmitri Fyodorovitch knocking again, since no one else could knock so savagely. She ran to the house-porter, who had already woken up and gone out to the gate, and begged him not to open it. But the man questioned Pyotr Ilyitch and learned that he wanted to see Fenya on very “important business,” and at last he made up his mind to open. Pyotr Ilyitch was let into Fenya’s kitchen, but the girl asked him to let the house-porter stay in the room, “because of her misgivings.” He began to question her and at once learned the most vital fact. When Dmitri Fyodorovitch ran out to look for Grushenka, he had snatched a pestle from the mortar. When he came back, he no longer had the pestle, and his hands were smeared with blood.

“And the blood was simply flowing, dripping from him, dripping!” Fenya kept exclaiming. This horrible detail was just a product of her overwrought imagination. But although the blood was not “dripping,” Pyotr Ilyitch had seen those bloodstained hands himself, and had helped to wash them. Besides, the question he had to settle was not how soon the blood had dried. It was where Dmitri Fyodorovitch had run with the pestle, or rather, whether it really was to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s, and how he could find that out for certain. Pyotr Ilyitch kept coming back to this point. He learned nothing conclusive, but he came away convinced that Dmitri Fyodorovitch could have gone nowhere but to his father’s house, and that something must therefore have happened there.

“And when he came back,” Fenya added excitedly, “I told him the whole story, and then I started asking him, ‘Why have you got blood on your hands, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?’ And he said it was human blood, and that he had just killed someone. He confessed it all to me, and suddenly ran off like a madman. I sat down and began to think, where’s he running off to now like a madman? He’ll go to Mokroe, I thought, and kill my mistress there. I ran out to beg him not to kill her. I was running to his lodgings, but I looked at Plotnikov’s shop and saw him just setting off, and there was no blood on his hands then.” (Fenya had noticed this and remembered it.) Fenya’s old grandmother confirmed her story as well as she could. Pyotr Ilyitch asked a few more questions and left the house even more upset and uneasy than when he had entered it.

The simplest and most direct thing for him to do would have been to go straight to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s and find out whether anything had happened there, and if so, what. Only after satisfying himself on that point would he go to the police captain, as he firmly intended to do. But the night was dark, Fyodor Pavlovitch’s gates were strong, and he would have to knock again. He hardly knew Fyodor Pavlovitch. What if they opened up after all his knocking, and nothing had happened? Then Fyodor Pavlovitch, in his jeering way, would tell the story all over town: how a stranger named Perhotin had broken in on him at midnight to ask whether anyone had killed him. It would be a scandal. And scandal was what Pyotr Ilyitch dreaded more than anything in the world.

Yet the feeling that possessed him was so strong that, though he stamped his foot angrily and swore at himself, he set off again, not to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s but to Madame Hohlakov’s. He decided that if she denied having just given Dmitri Fyodorovitch three thousand roubles, he would go straight to the police captain. If she admitted giving him the money, he would go home and let the matter rest until the next morning.

Of course, it is perfectly obvious that going at eleven o’clock at night to a fashionable lady who was a complete stranger, and perhaps getting her out of bed to ask her an amazing question, was even more likely to cause a scandal than going to Fyodor Pavlovitch. But that is just how it is sometimes, especially in cases like this one, with the decisions of the most precise and phlegmatic people. And Pyotr Ilyitch was far from phlegmatic at that moment. He remembered all his life how a haunting uneasiness gradually took hold of him, growing more and more painful and driving him on against his will. All the way he kept cursing himself, naturally, for going to this lady. But “I will get to the bottom of it, I will!” he repeated for the tenth time, grinding his teeth, and he carried out his plan.

It was exactly eleven o’clock when he entered Madame Hohlakov’s house. He was let into the yard fairly quickly, but when he asked whether the lady was still up, the porter could only say that she was usually in bed by that hour.
“Ask at the top of the stairs. If the lady wants to see you, she’ll see you. If she won’t, she won’t.”

Pyotr Ilyitch went up, but things were not so easy here. The footman did not want to take in his name, but at last he called a maid. Pyotr Ilyitch politely but firmly asked her to tell her mistress that an official living in the town, by the name of Perhotin, had called on particular business, and that he would not have dared to come if it were not of the greatest importance. “Tell her in those words, in those words exactly,” he told the girl.

She went away. He stayed waiting in the entry. Madame Hohlakov herself was already in her bedroom, though not yet asleep. She had felt upset ever since Mitya’s visit, and she had a presentiment that she would not get through the night without the sick headache that always came over her after such excitement. She was surprised when the maid gave her the message. She refused irritably to see him. Still, the unexpected visit at such an hour from an “official living in the town,” a total stranger, roused her feminine curiosity intensely. But this time Pyotr Ilyitch was as stubborn as a mule. He begged the maid most earnestly to carry another message, in these very words:
“That he had come on business of the greatest importance, and that Madame Hohlakov might have cause to regret it later if she refused to see him now.”
“I plunged headlong,” he said afterward, describing it.

The maid stared at him in amazement and went to deliver his message again. Madame Hohlakov was impressed. She thought for a little, asked what he looked like, and learned that he was “very well dressed, young and so polite.” I may mention in passing that Pyotr Ilyitch was a rather good-looking young man, and knew it. Madame Hohlakov made up her mind to see him. She was in her dressing-gown and slippers, but she threw a black shawl over her shoulders. “The official” was asked into the drawing-room, the very room where Mitya had been received a short while before. The lady came to meet her visitor with a stern, questioning look, and without asking him to sit down she began at once with the question:
“What do you want?”
“I have taken the liberty of disturbing you, madam, about our common acquaintance, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov,” Perhotin began.
But he had hardly said the name when the lady’s face showed acute irritation. She almost shrieked, and cut him off in a fury:

“How much longer am I to be pestered by that awful man?” she cried hysterically. “How dare you, sir, how could you take it on yourself to disturb a lady you don’t know, in her own house at such an hour!... And to force yourself on her to talk about a man who came here, to this very drawing-room, only three hours ago, to murder me, and went stamping out of the room, the way no one would leave a decent house. Let me tell you, sir, that I shall lodge a complaint against you, and I will not let it pass. Kindly leave me at once.... I am a mother.... I ... I—”
“Murder! So he tried to murder you, too?”
“Why, has he killed somebody else?” Madame Hohlakov asked impulsively.

“If you would kindly listen, madam, for half a moment, I’ll explain it all in a couple of words,” Perhotin answered firmly. “At five o’clock this afternoon Dmitri Fyodorovitch borrowed ten roubles from me, and I know for a fact he had no money. Yet at nine o’clock he came to see me with a bundle of hundred-rouble notes in his hand, about two or three thousand roubles. His hands and face were covered with blood, and he looked like a madman. I asked him where he had got so much money, and he answered that he had just received it from you, that you had given him three thousand to go to the gold-mines....”
Madame Hohlakov’s face took on an expression of intense and painful excitement.

“Good God! He must have killed his old father!” she cried, clasping her hands. “I have never given him money, never! Oh, run, run!... Don’t say another word! Save the old man ... run to his father ... run!”
“Excuse me, madam, so you did not give him money? You remember for a fact that you did not give him any money?”

“No, I didn’t, I didn’t! I refused to give it to him, because he couldn’t appreciate it. He ran out in a fury, stamping. He rushed at me, but I slipped away.... And let me tell you, since I want to hide nothing from you now, that he actually spat at me. Can you imagine that! But why are we standing? Ah, sit down.”
“Excuse me, I....”
“Or better, run, run, you must run and save the poor old man from an awful death!”
“But what if he has killed him already?”
“Ah, good heavens, yes! Then what are we to do now? What do you think we must do now?”

Meanwhile she had made Pyotr Ilyitch sit down, and she sat down facing him. Briefly but fairly clearly, Pyotr Ilyitch told her the story of the affair, or at least the part of it he had witnessed himself. He described his visit to Fenya, too, and told her about the pestle. All these details had an overwhelming effect on the distracted lady. She kept shrieking and covering her face with her hands....

“Would you believe it, I foresaw all this! I have that special gift, whatever I imagine comes true. And how often I’ve looked at that awful man and always thought, that man will end by murdering me. And now it’s happened ... that is, if he hasn’t murdered me, but only his own father, it’s only because the finger of God protected me. And what’s more, he was ashamed to murder me because, in this very place, I put the holy ikon from the relics of the holy martyr Saint Varvara on his neck.... And to think how near I was to death at that moment, I went close up to him and he stretched out his neck to me!... Do you know, Pyotr Ilyitch (I think you said your name was Pyotr Ilyitch), I don’t believe in miracles, but that ikon and this unmistakable miracle with me now—that shakes me, and I’m ready to believe in anything you like. Have you heard about Father Zossima?... But I don’t know what I’m saying ... and just imagine, with the ikon on his neck he spat at me.... He only spat, it’s true, he didn’t murder me and ... he dashed away! But what shall we do, what must we do now? What do you think?”
Pyotr Ilyitch got up and announced that he was going straight to the police captain to tell him all about it, and would leave him to do whatever he thought best.

“Oh, he’s an excellent man, excellent! Mihail Makarovitch, I know him. Of course, he’s the person to go to. How practical you are, Pyotr Ilyitch! How well you’ve thought of everything! In your place I should never have thought of it!”

“Especially as I know the police captain very well, too,” remarked Pyotr Ilyitch. He was still standing, and was plainly anxious to get away as quickly as he could from the impulsive lady, who would not let him say goodbye and leave.

“And be sure, be sure,” she prattled on, “to come back and tell me what you see there, and what you find out ... what comes to light ... how they’ll try him ... and what he’s sentenced to.... Tell me, we have no capital punishment, have we? But be sure to come, even if it’s at three o’clock at night, at four, at half-past four.... Tell them to wake me, to wake me, to shake me, if I don’t get up.... But, good heavens, I won’t sleep! But wait, wouldn’t it be better if I came with you?”
“N—no. But if you would write three lines in your own hand, saying that you did not give Dmitri Fyodorovitch money, it might perhaps be of use ... in case it’s needed....”

“Of course!” Madame Hohlakov skipped, delighted, over to her bureau. “And you know, I’m simply struck, amazed at your resourcefulness, your good sense in such matters. Are you in the service here? I’m delighted to think that you’re in the service here!”
And still talking, she scribbled the following lines on half a sheet of notepaper:

I’ve never in my life lent three thousand roubles today to that unhappy man, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov (for, in spite of everything, he is unhappy). I’ve never given him money, never: That I swear by all that’s holy!
K. HOHLAKOV.
“Here’s the note!” she said, turning quickly to Pyotr Ilyitch. “Go, save him. It’s a noble deed on your part!”
And she made the sign of the cross over him three times. She ran out to see him to the passage.

“How grateful I am to you! You can’t think how grateful I am to you for coming to me first. How is it I haven’t met you before? I shall feel flattered to see you at my house in the future. How delightful that you are living here!... Such precision! Such practical ability!... They must appreciate you, they must understand you. If there’s anything I can do, believe me ... oh, I love young people! I’m in love with young people! The younger generation are the one prop of our suffering country. Her one hope.... Oh, go, go!...”

But Pyotr Ilyitch had already run off, or she would not have let him go so soon. Still, Madame Hohlakov had made a rather agreeable impression on him, which had somewhat softened his worry at being dragged into such an unpleasant affair. Tastes differ, as we all know. “She’s by no means so elderly,” he thought, feeling pleased. “On the contrary, I would have taken her for her daughter.”

As for Madame Hohlakov, she was simply enchanted by the young man. “Such sense! Such exactness! In so young a man! In our day! And all that with such manners and looks! People say the young people of today are no good for anything, but here’s an example!” and so on. So she simply forgot this “dreadful affair,” and only as she was getting into bed, suddenly recalling “how near death she had been,” did she exclaim: “Ah, it is awful, awful!”
But she fell at once into a sound, sweet sleep.

I would not, however, have dwelt on such trivial and irrelevant details if this eccentric meeting between the young official and the by no means elderly widow had not later turned out to be the foundation of the whole career of that practical and precise young man. His story is remembered to this day with amazement in our town, and perhaps I shall have something to say about it when I have finished my long history of the Brothers Karamazov.
